newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta set to seal or break union with Europe.
newsitem.headline: Malta set to seal or break union with Europe.

text.p: The people of Malta vote on Saturday in a general election described by the prime minister as a referendum on the island's membership of the European Union.

Divided between two mainstream parties with usually only 5,000 votes deciding victory or defeat, the Mediterranean island's electorate of 275,000 is being urged to embrace Europe or ease back into "positive neutrality".

Malta applied for membership in 1990 under Prime Minister Edward Fenech Adami, 62, who told Reuters on Friday: "I already have a mandate...(but) it will be a sort of another referendum on Malta's membership of the EU."
Exuding confidence in victory over the Labour Party, he added: "It will be clear that Malta's people have chosen to be members of the EU."

Labour, led by Alfred Sant, 48, will kill Malta's bid to join. Sant says many EU rules would hit the small island with costs it can not afford. He vows to dismantle value added tax and, by consequence, withdraw Malta's application.
"We should have a special relationship, not membership...I would like to see security, not military, cooperation, for example on drugs, contraband and the movement of people."
At mass meetings throughout the Mediterranean island, the leaders and some 300 candidates for the 65-seat parliament have focused on peoples' pockets and, by extension, Europe.
Fenech Adami's Nationalist Party, which had a three-seat margin in the last parliament and a record 13,000-vote majority, say that membership will ensure economic prosperity.
"We will be able to open our doors without restriction to a market of 314 million people," said Fenech Adami.
His party says its management of the economy, based mainly on manufacturing and tourism, has seen growth at some six percent a year and brought unemployment down to 3.2 percent.
It adds that EU membership could mean assistance of Lm43 million ($118 million) a year and give "reassuring awareness that we have the security of a group of European countries."
For Sant membership conflicts with Malta's neutrality.
While tensions have eased in Europe they have not vanished in the Mediterranean between north and south, "especially with the growth of (Islamic) fundamentalism", he said.
Labour, long uneasy about increased visits to the island by Western naval ships, is committed to pulling Malta out of NATO's Partnership for Peace Programme which it joined in 1995.
Malta has no independent opinion polls and few will forecast the outcome of the vote.
"There is a possibility that no major party will achieve an absolute majority of votes...which has not happened in Malta since 1966," the Malta Independent wrote.

The "wild card" could be the Alternattiva Demokratikanotes (Democratic Alternative) which won no seats at the last election in February 1992. It favours EU membership in principle but says a final decision should only be taken in a referendum.

Some 500 polling stations on Malta and the sister island of Gozo open at 7 a.m. on Saturday and close at 10 p.m. Malta's system of proportional representation means results are not expected until late on Sunday or early on Monday.
